problem: If $f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡z,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y,z)$ from $(1,0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(0,1,1).$
worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡z)\,\text{d}y-y\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(1,0,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(1,0,\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)\,\text{d}x+(1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))\,\text{d}y-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}z \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y+0\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(1+Δx,0+Δy,\frac{\pi }{2}+Δz),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+1\,Δy+0\,Δz.
$$

Moving from $(1,0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(0,1,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =0-1=-1, \\ Δy & =1-0=1 \\ Δz & =1-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\,Δx+1\,Δy+0\,Δz \\  & ≈0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot (1)+0\cdot (1-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & ≈1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y,z)$ increases by approximately $1.$
